title: Rivergate and Horizon
premise: Tamsin Dunmore, a railroad engineer who vanished into the closed lines of the Rivergate valley seven years ago, learns that the survey crew he once led has gone silent above the falls. Their last radio message mentions the Horizon, a salvage ship carrying documents that could clear his name—and expose the men who framed him for a disaster that killed eleven workers. Racing the salvage fleet upriver through six tides of rapids, fog, and sabotage, Tamsin must decide whether reclaiming his identity is worth surrendering the invisible life he built. In the end, he reaches the wreck at low tide, chooses justice over vindication by giving the evidence to the victims' families rather than the courts, and returns to Rivergate no longer hiding—but no longer the man he was either.
about_author: Yara Fairweather is a former hydrographic surveyor who spent a decade charting forgotten river routes before turning to fiction. She writes adventure stories about people who measure the world precisely but trust it reluctantly.

chapters.title: Miles, Not Years
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Seven years after fleeing Rivergate, he works the closed rail lines, mapping decay and living under a borrowed name. A routine survey of the old trestle reveals fresh survey stakes that aren't his. The emotional beat is quiet unease: the past has begun measuring him back.

chapters.title: The Silence Above the Falls
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A river pilot named Odile Brack brings word that the Dunmore Survey crew—men Tamsin trained—stopped answering radio three days ago above Kestrel Falls. Their last transmission mentioned the salvage ship Horizon. Tamsin's instinct is to stay hidden; his conscience refuses. He decides to go.

chapters.title: Six Tides
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Odile explains the river's rhythm: the wreck can only be reached at low tide windows, and the salvage fleet will arrive with the sixth. Tamsin calculates a route through the closed locks. The beat is cold resolve—he trades invisibility for a countdown.

chapters.title: The Man in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She reveals she knew Tamsin's real name all along and has her own grudge: her brother died in the collapse Tamsin was blamed for. She agrees to pilot him anyway. The beat is uneasy alliance built on shared grief and mutual suspicion.

chapters.title: Closed Lines
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They slip through the abandoned lock system at night, Tamsin's engineering knowledge the only key. Sabotage is discovered: the third lock's gears have been stripped deliberately. Someone knows he's coming. The beat is the first spike of fear.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. They find the survey crew's supply cache ransacked, one man—young Ferro—hiding in a culvert, half-starved. He tells them the crew found documents aboard the wreck before the Horizon's advance party scattered them. The beat is dread sharpening into urgency.

chapters.title: The Wreck of the Meridian Star
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ferro describes the wreck: the Meridian Star, a salvage vessel that sank carrying the inquiry records Tamsin needs. Tamsin realizes the disaster he fled was engineered, and the proof has been sitting in the river for seven years. The beat is vertigo—his whole exile reframed.

chapters.title: Fleet on the Horizon
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Through field glasses they spot the salvage fleet, two tides ahead of schedule, moving fast under a private flag. Odile recognizes the financier aboard: Aldous Crane, the man who profited from the collapse. The beat is the race becoming real.

chapters.title: Portage
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The sabotaged lock forces them to haul the boat overland through the gorge. Ferro, weak and guilt-ridden for leading the fleet's scouts to the crew, earns a measure of trust. The beat is fragile camaraderie forged by labor.

chapters.title: Radio Ghosts
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. At a relay station they intercept a transmission: two of Tamsin's crew are alive, held aboard the Horizon as leverage until Crane confirms the documents are destroyed. Tamsin hears his old foreman's voice and nearly breaks cover. The beat is temptation versus discipline.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Half Tide
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. To reach the falls ahead of the fleet, they must cross a condemned rail bridge Tamsin himself inspected years ago. He calculates its failure point and they cross with minutes to spare as it folds into the river. The beat is exhilarating competence—engineering as survival.

chapters.title: Crane's Offer
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A parley boat intercepts them; Crane's agent offers Tamsin money, a pardon, his name back—if he surrenders Ferro and walks away. Tamsin refuses, but the offer plants a poisonous question: what if justice and his own redemption are different things? The beat is moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Kestrel Falls
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. They portage the falls in fog while the fleet's engines echo behind them. Ferro confesses the crew found not just documents but the wreck's logbook, proving Crane ordered the Meridian Star scuttled with the inquiry aboard. The beat is the truth fully assembled.

chapters.title: Fourth Tide
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They reach the wreck site at low tide and begin diving in the flooded cargo hold. Tamsin finds the sealed document case—and the bones of the inquiry clerk who died protecting it. The beat is solemn: the dead have been waiting for him.

chapters.title: The Fleet Arrives Early
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The Horizon rounds the bend a full tide ahead of schedule, tipped off by a traitor among the river pilots. Odile realizes the betrayal traces to her own harbor master. The beat is fury and the collapse of her last illusions about home.

chapters.title: Flooded Hold
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Boarding parties swarm the wreck as the tide turns. Tamsin and Ferro seal themselves in the hold, using the sinking ship's own ballast system against the boarders. The beat is claustrophobic cat-and-mouse, Tamsin's engineering turned into a weapon.

chapters.title: The Foreman's Voice
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Cornered, Tamsin faces his captured foreman, Halloway, who confesses he testified against Tamsin seven years ago under Crane's threats. The confrontation is bitter and human: no clean villains, only frightened men. The beat is grief that finally has somewhere to go.

chapters.title: Fifth Tide, Rising
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. With the wreck flooding and the Horizon's cranes tearing at the hull, Odile executes a desperate plan: scuttle a derelict barge across the channel, stranding the fleet's boarding parties. The beat is audacity—she out-salvages the salvagers.

chapters.title: The Choice at Low Water
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The climax. Tamsin escapes the wreck with the documents as Crane himself confronts him on the mudflats, offering everything one last time. Tamsin realizes the courts Crane owns can never deliver justice—so he gives the evidence to Odile, to carry to the victims' families, and lets Crane believe he's won. The beat is self-erasure as an act of strength.

chapters.title: Sixth Tide
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. As the fleet celebrates and Crane departs, the families of Rivergate receive the logbook and documents. Odile watches the first arrests happen at the harbor while Tamsin slips away upriver, refusing credit. The beat is justice arriving quietly, outside the law's front door.

chapters.title: The Name on the Manifest
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Weeks later, Tamsin signs his real name to a survey manifest for the first time in seven years—not to be forgiven, but to stand as himself. Halloway's testimony and the families' case proceed without him. The beat is quiet reclamation: identity as a choice, not a verdict.

chapters.title: Rivergate and Horizon
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Spring comes to Rivergate; the locks reopen under new, honest management, and Odile takes the pilot's chair she never wanted until she earned it. A stranger with a familiar stride walks the repaired trestle at dawn. She doesn't call out. The beat is earned peace—some returns need no words.
